body: The Airbus A330 has earned an unusual nickname among aviation enthusiasts: the "Butter Machine." The name comes from its reputation for exceptionally smooth landings, often marked by a gentle first contact between the rear wheels and the runway before the rest of the landing gear settles. According to Flightradar24, the A330 is often called 'The Butter Machine' because of its smooth landings, and it names the main landing gear as the jet's easiest identifier: two sets of four wheels, tilted backward. Canada's Transportation Safety Board (TSB) describes the same arrangement in an A330 investigation report: each bogie carries four wheels in a twin-tandem layout, and the bogies are inclined so the rear tires touch the runway first. Flightradar24 adds that the four-engine A340 carries an extra center landing gear, while the A330 relies on its two main bogies alone.

That arrangement becomes more interesting once the wheels meet the runway. According to the same report, forces are transferred gradually when the wheels touch down, instead of arriving through all eight main tires at once. The supporting cast includes oleo-pneumatic shock absorbers, a balanced bogie design, titanium and corrosion-resistant steel, and two landing gear control units that alternate for reliability. The job of positioning the bogie before touchdown belongs to a hydraulic ram called a pitch trimmer. Pilots and engineers on the PPRuNe forum describe it as the part that sets the bogie nose-up when the gear is selected down, and a research paper on tire heat at touchdown says it lifts the front wheels of the bogie and lets the rear wheels descend around the bogie beam. A patent for a variable-damping pitch trimmer explains that the actuator positions the wheels before touchdown, helps stow the gear, and also damps the motion of the bogie beam relative to the leg, while a shortening mechanism pulls the shock absorber up inside the leg during retraction so the gear fits into a compact bay.

The reason for the angle is less settled than the nickname might suggest. In a PPRuNe thread on landing gear lean, a contributor insists that simple geometry points to storage, noting that the tilt exists so the bogie fits the bay. Another poster counters that the A330 and A340 are a special case, claiming the nose-up tilt is intentional and works a bit like the semi-levered gear on the Boeing 777-300ER, improving clearance under the aft fuselage. The Points Guy reports that wheel orientation is mostly a space-saving choice, even though pilots generally agree that trailing-link gear produces the most flattering landings. In other words, the tilt may exist for storage, yet it still shapes the touchdown.

Once the aircraft is close to the runway, the flight-control system and the wing become just as important. According to the Australian Transport Safety Bureau, flare mode replaces the normal load-factor law with a flare law, letting crews use the same landing technique as on non-fly-by-wire aircraft. Airbus' own Safety First magazine says the flare should begin around 40 feet (12 meters) above the runway on the A330, A340, A350 and A380, compared with 30 feet (nine meters) on smaller Airbus jets. On a PPRuNe thread about hard A330 landings, pilots describe how the aircraft can touch down beautifully on the rear wheels, then float along the runway before the front wheels come down heavily. Their advice is to touch down on the rear wheels, then pitch down firmly enough to bring the front wheels gently onto the runway while speed remains, which is exactly what they say the autopilot does on an autoland. The same principles appear on later widebodies: the A350-1000's six-wheel bogie is built so the rear wheels typically touch down first, and the A380 needs 20 tires on its main gear. Airbus also launched the A330neo with new engines and winglets that improved per-seat fuel economy by 14 percent, while the landing gear that helped create the Butter Machine reputation remains fundamentally part of the family.
en.summary: The Airbus A330 is known among enthusiasts as the "Butter Machine" for its exceptionally smooth landings. The secret lies in its tilted four-wheel bogies, which touch down rear wheels first, helped by a pitch trimmer and flare law — though experts still disagree on why the gear is tilted in the first place.
en.title: Why the Airbus A330 lands so smoothly: the 'Butter Machine' engineering behind its tilted gear

body: 空中巴士A330在航迷之間有個特別的綽號：「奶油機」。這個名稱來自它異常平穩的降落：主起落架的後輪往往先輕觸跑道，其餘機輪再逐漸著地。據Flightradar24指出，A330常因平穩降落而被稱為「奶油機」，而它最容易辨認的特徵正是主起落架：兩組各四輪的小車架向後傾斜。加拿大運輸安全委員會（TSB）在一份A330調查報告中也有相同描述：每個小車架以雙串列方式配置四輪，車架傾斜使後輪先觸地；相較之下，四發動機的A340還多一組中央起落架，A330僅靠兩組主小車架，因此這兩組裝置的表現格外受關注。

車架傾斜的真正作用，在於讓著陸力量分段傳遞。同一份報告指出，機輪觸地時力量是逐漸傳遞的，而非一次由8個主輪同時承受。輔助的零件還包括油氣式減震支柱、平衡式小車架設計、鈦合金與耐腐蝕鋼材，以及兩組交替運作以提升可靠度的起落架控制單元。讓小車架在觸地前保持傾斜的，是一具名為俯仰配平器的液壓作動器：它在起落架放下時把小車架設定為前輪上揚；一篇關於觸地輪胎生熱的研究指出，它會抬起小車架前輪、讓後輪繞著小車架橫梁下降，同一研究也提到它能發揮減震作用。一項可變阻尼俯仰配平器專利則說明，該作動器能在觸地前定位機輪、協助收起落架，同時抑制小車架橫梁相對於支柱的運動；收放過程中另有縮短機構把減震支柱拉入支柱內部，使起落架收進較小的收納艙。

不過，車架向後傾斜的原始用途，在專家之間並無定論。飛行員論壇PPRuNe上有參與者主張，單純從幾何結構看，傾斜是為了讓小車架收進機艙；另一名發文者則反駁，A330與A340是特例，鼻輪上揚的傾斜是刻意設計，作用類似波音777-300ER的半槓桿式起落架，有助於改善後機身下方的淨空。The Points Guy則報導，機輪方向多半是節省空間的選擇，儘管飛行員普遍認為拖曳連桿式起落架最能帶來漂亮的降落。換言之，傾斜可能源於收納需求，卻仍會影響觸地感受；對設計者而言，一項收納方案同時帶來舒適效果並不衝突。

觸地前最後幾秒，飛控系統與機翼同樣關鍵。據澳洲運輸安全局指出，A330的拉平模式會以拉平法則取代正常的負載係數法則，讓機組能以與非線傳飛控飛機相同的技巧降落。空中巴士《Safety First》雜誌指出，A330、A340、A350與A380的拉平應在跑道上方約40英尺（12公尺）開始，小型空中巴士噴射機則為30英尺（9公尺）；進場坡度陡於標準3度時，可能需要更早拉平。即使如此，漂亮的後輪觸地並不保證全程平穩：飛行員在論壇上描述，飛機可能以後輪優雅觸地、再沿跑道滑行一段後，前輪重重落下；他們的建議是先以後輪觸地，再確實下俯使前輪在速度仍足時輕柔著地，最後才使用反推力——這正是自動落地時自動駕駛的做法。同一套邏輯也延續到更新的廣體機：A350-1000的六輪小車架同樣以後輪先觸地，A380主起落架則有多達20條輪胎；A330neo換裝新發動機與翼梢小翼後，每座位燃油效率提升14%，但讓「奶油機」聲名遠播的起落架，本質上仍是這個家族的一部分。
zh.summary: 空中巴士A330以異常平穩的降落聞名，被航迷稱為「奶油機」。關鍵在於四輪小車架向後傾斜、後輪先觸地，加上俯仰配平器與拉平法則的配合；不過傾斜的原始用途在專家間仍無定論。
zh.title: 為什麼A330降落特別平穩？從後輪先觸地到俯仰配平器的「奶油機」工程
